item.content:encoded:
The Australian Embassy in The Hague is seeking a highly capable and analytical professional to join the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) as a Policy and Research Officer – LE4. This is a 12-month non-ongoing position for a locally engaged staff member, supporting Australia’s engagement with major international legal, accountability and diplomatic institutions based in The Hague. The position provides an opportunity to contribute to Australia’s international policy interests, particularly in relation to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), International Criminal Court (ICC), international law, human rights, political affairs, accountability mechanisms and the ongoing international response to the July 2014 downing of flight MH17. Importantly, applicants must already have the legal right to live and work in the Netherlands. The Australian Embassy in The Hague cannot provide visa sponsorship or relocation assistance, and applications from individuals without an appropriate and valid Dutch residence and work permit will not be considered.

Opportunity Overview

The Policy and Research Officer will work within the Australian Embassy in The Hague and assist the Australian Government in advancing its interests across international organisations and institutions located in The Hague.

The role is particularly relevant to professionals with experience or qualifications in areas such as:

  • International relations
  • International law
  • Political affairs
  • Human rights
  • Policy research
  • Government and diplomacy
  • International organisations
  • Legal research and analysis
  • Accountability and justice mechanisms

The successful applicant will be engaged on a non-ongoing 12-month contract as a Locally Engaged Staff member.

The employment conditions for Locally Engaged Staff are governed by the laws of the Netherlands. The Fair Work Act 2009 does not apply to the employment of Locally Engaged Staff at Australia’s overseas diplomatic and consular missions.

About the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) is responsible for advancing the interests of Australia and Australians internationally.

Its responsibilities include strengthening Australia’s security, supporting Australia’s economic prosperity, delivering Australia’s overseas development assistance and helping Australian citizens travelling or living overseas.

DFAT provides foreign, trade and development policy advice to the Australian Government and works with other Australian Government agencies to coordinate Australia’s global, regional and bilateral interests.

Working at an Australian diplomatic mission therefore provides exposure to Australia’s international policy and diplomatic activities while supporting government priorities in a particular country or region.

About the Policy and Research Officer Position

The Australian Government is looking for a Policy and Research Officer to support Australia’s engagement with international organisations based in The Hague.

The Hague is home to a number of important international legal and accountability institutions, making this position particularly relevant to professionals interested in international law, diplomacy, international justice and government policy.

The successful candidate will assist with Australia’s engagement with institutions including:

  • The International Court of Justice (ICJ)
  • The International Criminal Court (ICC)
  • The Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH)
  • The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA)
  • Other international legal and accountability bodies and institutions

The Officer will undertake research and analysis, prepare briefings and reports, monitor developments, support meetings and visits, develop professional networks and provide broader policy and administrative assistance to the Embassy.

MH17 Accountability Work

One of the significant areas of responsibility associated with this position is supporting Australia’s ongoing pursuit of accountability relating to the July 2014 downing of flight MH17.

The Officer will monitor and report on relevant legal developments and support Australia’s participation in ongoing accountability efforts and commemorative activities.

The role may also involve work on international law, political affairs, human rights and budget-related issues, depending on Australia’s priorities and the needs of the Embassy.

This makes the position particularly suitable for candidates who have a strong interest in international justice, accountability, international legal proceedings and Australia’s role in international institutions.

Key Responsibilities

The Policy and Research Officer will be responsible for a broad range of policy, research, representational and organisational duties.

1. Support engagement with international legal institutions

The Officer will support Australia’s engagement with the ICJ, ICC and other international legal and accountability organisations.

This may involve:

  • Conducting research and analysis
  • Preparing briefing materials
  • Providing administrative support
  • Supporting effective governance
  • Preparing information to advance Australian Government priorities
  • Monitoring institutional developments
  • Supporting Australia’s participation in relevant meetings and processes

The Officer must therefore be capable of understanding complex information and converting it into useful, accurate and concise material for government decision-makers and other stakeholders.

2. Monitor international developments

A key component of the role is monitoring developments that may affect Australia’s interests.

The successful candidate will research, analyse and report on developments in areas including:

  • International law
  • International politics
  • Accountability
  • Human rights
  • Hague-based international organisations
  • Other international policy issues relevant to Australia

The ability to identify important developments, understand their implications and communicate them effectively will be essential.

3. Represent the Australian Embassy

The Officer may be required to represent the Embassy at meetings involving international organisations based in The Hague.

These organisations may include the Hague Conference on Private International Law and the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

This responsibility requires strong interpersonal and representational skills, professionalism and the ability to communicate Australia’s interests appropriately in an international environment.

4. Support MH17-related accountability efforts

The successful candidate will monitor developments related to MH17 and assist with Australia’s participation in ongoing accountability activities.

Responsibilities may include:

  • Monitoring legal developments
  • Preparing reports and briefings
  • Supporting Australia’s participation in accountability processes
  • Assisting with commemorative activities
  • Communicating relevant developments internally

5. Build and maintain professional networks

The Officer will establish, maintain and develop a network of contacts capable of providing useful information and supporting Australia’s interests.

This requires strong relationship-building skills and the ability to work effectively with internal and external stakeholders.

6. Coordinate visits and briefings

The position may involve coordinating visit programs and managing briefings for Australian Government officials and high-level visitors.

The Officer must therefore be able to manage competing tasks, coordinate stakeholders and deliver accurate information within strict deadlines.

7. Provide broader Embassy support

The role may also include administrative, public diplomacy and policy support.

In emergency situations, the Officer may also be required to provide consular assistance.

This means applicants should be adaptable and comfortable working across different responsibilities in a small diplomatic mission.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants should have a tertiary qualification in international relations, law or another relevant field, or an equivalent level of professional experience.

The ideal candidate should demonstrate:

Strong research and analytical skills

Applicants should be able to conduct detailed research, evaluate information from different sources, identify relevant findings and produce accurate analysis.

Knowledge of international law is specifically relevant to the position.

Excellent communication skills

The role requires strong oral and written communication abilities.

Applicants should be able to prepare professional documents that present information in a logical, concise and persuasive manner.

English is essential, while Dutch is desirable.

Strong interpersonal and liaison skills

The Officer will interact with government officials, international organisations and other stakeholders.

Applicants should therefore be capable of establishing professional relationships, maintaining networks and communicating effectively with people from different organisations and backgrounds.

Strong organisational abilities

The successful candidate will need to manage several responsibilities simultaneously, meet tight deadlines and maintain accuracy while working under limited supervision.

Ability to work independently

Although the role involves working as part of a small team, applicants must be capable of taking initiative and completing tasks with limited supervision.

Security Clearance Requirements

This is a security-designated position.

The successful applicant must either already hold an Australian Government NV1 security clearance or have the ability to obtain one.

Applicants must also be willing to undergo the security checks required to obtain an Australian National Security clearance.

Importantly, the vacancy specifies that applications can only be considered from nationals of:

  • Australia
  • Canada
  • New Zealand
  • United Kingdom
  • United States

Applicants must be eligible for an Australian Government security clearance.

The position also specifies that candidates who hold dual Dutch nationality together with one of the listed nationalities are not eligible for the security clearance required for this position.

Applicants should carefully consider this requirement before applying.

Right to Live and Work in the Netherlands

A mandatory requirement for this position is an existing legal right to live and work in the Netherlands.

The Australian Embassy in The Hague:

  • Does not provide visa sponsorship
  • Does not assist with relocation
  • Will not consider applications without an appropriate and valid visa or permit
  • Requires successful applicants to meet Dutch legal requirements for employment

Any costs associated with taking up the position, including relocation expenses, are the responsibility of the successful candidate.

This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because meeting the nationality requirement alone does not automatically make someone eligible to apply.

Selection Criteria

Applicants must respond to each of the five listed selection criteria as part of their application.

Each response has a strict maximum of 250 words.

Applications may not be assessed if they are incomplete or if responses exceed the specified word limit.

Selection Criterion A: Communication

Applicants must demonstrate well-developed written and oral communication skills in English and Dutch for both traditional and digital platforms in a professional environment.

Candidates should provide examples demonstrating their ability to prepare written material that presents information logically, succinctly and persuasively.

Selection Criterion B: Research and Analysis

Applicants must demonstrate the ability to independently conduct high-quality, thorough and accurate research using a variety of sources, including data.

Candidates should demonstrate how they have analysed findings, monitored trends and presented research findings or reports to different internal and external stakeholders.

Selection Criterion C: Stakeholder Engagement

Applicants must demonstrate the ability to communicate and liaise effectively with internal and external stakeholders.

Relevant examples should show excellent interpersonal skills, the ability to establish effective stakeholder relationships and the capacity to build and maintain professional networks.

Selection Criterion D: Judgment and Problem-Solving

Applicants should demonstrate effective judgment, decision-making and complex problem-solving skills.

Candidates should provide examples showing their ability to use initiative and innovation when addressing challenges or developing solutions.

Selection Criterion E: Planning and Organisation

Applicants must demonstrate effective planning and organisational skills.

Examples should show the ability to manage multiple tasks and competing priorities, achieve required outcomes and meet tight deadlines while working with limited supervision.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Because the application requires a response to five specific selection criteria, applicants should avoid submitting generic statements.

A strong application should use specific examples from previous professional, academic or relevant experience.

For each selection criterion, candidates should consider using a structured example that clearly explains:

  1. The situation or context.
  2. The task or responsibility they were given.
  3. The actions they personally took.
  4. The result or outcome achieved.
  5. What the example demonstrates about their suitability for the position.

Candidates should also ensure that each response remains within the 250-word limit.

It is important to address every part of the criterion rather than simply describing general skills.

English and Dutch Language Skills

English is explicitly identified as essential for the position, while Dutch is desirable.

However, the selection criteria request evidence of written and oral communication skills in both English and Dutch.

Applicants should therefore carefully review their own language capabilities and demonstrate relevant professional communication experience where applicable.

Dutch language ability may be particularly useful when interacting with local stakeholders and navigating the Dutch professional environment.

Locally Engaged Staff at Australian Overseas Missions

The position forms part of Australia’s Locally Engaged Staff workforce.

Locally Engaged Staff support and complement Australian Public Service employees working at Australia’s overseas posts.

They provide valuable local and professional knowledge, skills, networks and continuity across Australia’s diplomatic missions.

Australian Government overseas posts operate in more than 100 locations around the world, and locally engaged employees make an important contribution to Australia’s international objectives.

The position therefore offers an opportunity to contribute directly to the work of an Australian diplomatic mission while working in an international environment.

Recruitment and Application Process

The Human Resources Section based at the Australian High Commission in London manages recruitment processes for Australian diplomatic missions and other Australian Government overseas positions across the European region.

Applicants should use the Apply button associated with the vacancy to submit their application.

Questions regarding the recruitment process can be directed to the Human Resources Section at the recruitment contact provided in the vacancy announcement.

Applicants should ensure that their application is complete and that every selection criterion has been addressed within the required word limit.

Inclusive Workplace

The Australian Embassy states that it is committed to providing an inclusive and diverse workplace in which employees are valued.

Applications are encouraged from people with diverse backgrounds who share the values of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

Candidates should therefore focus their applications on demonstrating relevant skills, experience, qualifications and their ability to contribute effectively to the role.

Important Points Applicants Should Know

Before applying, candidates should carefully consider the following requirements:

  • The position is a 12-month non-ongoing contract.
  • It is a Locally Engaged Staff position at the Australian Embassy in The Hague.
  • Applicants must already have the legal right to live and work in the Netherlands.
  • The Australian Embassy does not provide visa sponsorship.
  • The Embassy does not provide relocation assistance.
  • Relocation and other costs associated with taking up the position are the responsibility of the successful applicant.
  • Applicants must meet the specified nationality requirements for the security clearance.
  • Eligible applicants must be nationals of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom or the United States.
  • Dual Dutch nationals who also hold one of the listed nationalities are stated to be ineligible for the required security clearance.
  • Applicants must be able to obtain an Australian Government NV1 security clearance.
  • Applicants must be willing to undergo the required security checks.
  • A tertiary qualification in international relations, law or another relevant field, or equivalent experience, is required.
  • Knowledge of international law is relevant to the position.
  • English communication skills are essential.
  • Dutch is desirable and is also referenced in the selection criteria.
  • Each selection criterion must be answered.
  • Each selection criterion has a strict 250-word limit.
  • Incomplete applications or responses exceeding the word limit may not be assessed.

Apply HERE 

Deadline

No application deadline is provided in the information supplied for this vacancy.

Applicants should therefore check the official vacancy page and application portal for the current closing date before submitting an application, as recruitment timelines can change.

Why This Position Could Be Valuable for International Policy Professionals

This opportunity is particularly relevant to professionals seeking experience at the intersection of international law, diplomacy, policy research, international organisations and government affairs.

Working in The Hague can provide exposure to an international environment where major institutions dealing with international justice, arbitration, private international law and accountability are located.

The responsibilities also extend beyond desk-based research. The successful applicant may participate in meetings, represent the Embassy, develop professional networks, coordinate high-level visits and support Australia’s engagement with international institutions.

For a professional with the appropriate nationality, Dutch work authorisation, qualifications and security-clearance eligibility, the role could provide meaningful experience in Australia’s international policy and diplomatic environment.

About the Commonwealth Government of Australia

The Commonwealth Government of Australia employs staff overseas to support the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and other Australian Government agencies at embassies, high commissions and consulates around the world.

These overseas employees contribute to Australia’s diplomatic, policy, consular and international objectives.

Locally Engaged Staff are an important part of this global workforce. Their knowledge, skills, networks and continuity help Australian diplomatic missions operate effectively in their host countries.

The Human Resources Section at the Australian High Commission in London manages local job vacancies across the European region, including various categories of employment and certain internship programs.

Learn more HERE

Privacy and Personal Data

Personal information provided during the recruitment process will be handled in accordance with the relevant privacy notice and applicable data protection laws.

Applicants should review the applicable privacy information before submitting personal details as part of their application.

Conclusion

The Policy and Research Officer – LE4 position at the Australian Embassy in The Hague offers an opportunity for an appropriately qualified and security-clearance-eligible professional to contribute to Australia’s international policy interests in one of the world’s most important centres for international law and justice. The successful candidate will support Australia’s engagement with institutions such as the International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court, monitor international legal and political developments, conduct research and analysis, prepare briefings, represent the Embassy at relevant meetings, support MH17 accountability activities and build relationships with international stakeholders. However, applicants should pay particularly close attention to the eligibility requirements. The position requires an existing right to live and work in the Netherlands, does not provide visa sponsorship or relocation assistance, and has specific nationality and security-clearance requirements. Candidates who meet these conditions and can demonstrate strong research, analytical, communication, stakeholder-management, judgment and organisational skills should prepare carefully structured responses to all five selection criteria, ensuring that every response remains within the strict 250-word limit. Because the supplied vacancy information does not state a closing date, prospective applicants should verify the official application portal for the current deadline and submit a complete application as early as possible.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the LASR Labs Winter 2027 cohort, a 13-week technical AI safety research programme designed for people interested in addressing some of the most important risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence.

The programme, run by London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs, focuses on action-relevant research into concrete AI safety threat models, particularly the risks associated with advanced AI systems and potential loss of human control over increasingly capable models.

Selected participants will work full-time and in person in London, joining research teams of three to four people under the supervision of experienced AI safety researchers. Over the course of the programme, participants will develop an AI safety research project from an initial proposal through experimentation, analysis and publication.

The Winter 2027 cohort will run from 11 January to 9 April 2027, and successful participants will receive a £15,000 stipend to support their living expenses in London. LASR Labs will also provide food, office space and travel support during the programme.

Application deadline: 20 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT.

About the LASR Labs Winter 2027 Programme

London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs is a technical research programme focused on reducing risks from advanced artificial intelligence. Its work concentrates on specific, action-relevant questions rather than AI safety as a broad or purely theoretical field.

The programme provides participants with an opportunity to gain hands-on experience conducting technical AI safety research while working alongside researchers and organisations within London’s AI safety ecosystem.

Participants are placed into teams of approximately three to four people and work under the guidance of an experienced supervisor. The objective is to take a research question from the early stages of project development through experimentation, iteration and eventual publication.

This makes the programme particularly valuable for applicants who want to transition into AI safety research, strengthen their technical research capabilities, build a publication record or explore a long-term career in AI safety.

Programme Dates and Duration

The Winter 2027 LASR Labs programme will take place over 13 weeks, from:

  • Start date: 11 January 2027
  • End date: 9 April 2027
  • Duration: 13 weeks
  • Format: Full-time and in person
  • Location: London, United Kingdom
  • Application deadline: 20 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT

The programme is run three times a year, giving participants multiple opportunities to engage with LASR Labs’ research environment.

What Does the LASR Labs Programme Offer?

One of the programme’s central strengths is its emphasis on taking participants through the entire research process rather than limiting them to theoretical learning.

The programme is divided broadly into an introductory Week 0 and a subsequent 12-week research period.

Week 0: Research Prioritisation and Project Selection

During the initial week, participants will be introduced to a selection of technical AI safety research projects.

With support from LASR Labs, participants will critically examine different research ideas and consider questions such as the following:

  • What makes a research project promising?
  • Which AI safety problems are particularly important?
  • What approaches could generate useful evidence?
  • How can researchers assess whether a research direction is likely to contribute meaningfully to AI safety?
  • What different AI safety research agendas exist?
  • How can researchers identify potential routes from research outputs to real-world impact?

Participants will then indicate their preferences regarding the available projects.

LASR Labs will use these preferences to form research teams and match participants with projects and supervisors.

This initial stage is designed to help participants develop research prioritisation skills, which LASR Labs considers important for producing useful and impactful AI safety research.

The 12-Week Research Project

After the introductory week, participants spend the remaining 12 weeks working with their teams to develop their selected research project.

The research process can involve:

  1. Developing and refining the research question.
  2. Formulating a research proposal.
  3. Designing experiments.
  4. Implementing technical approaches.
  5. Running experiments.
  6. Analysing results.
  7. Iterating based on findings.
  8. Developing conclusions and implications.
  9. Writing a research paper.
  10. Preparing the work for publication.

The expected output can take the form of a preprint, workshop paper or conference paper, accompanied by a blog post explaining the research and its significance.

Participants meet regularly with their supervisors throughout the programme. LASR staff also provide support with research planning and progress.

This structure gives participants practical experience with the full research lifecycle, from identifying and defining a problem to communicating findings to a wider technical audience.

£15,000 Stipend and Other Programme Benefits

A major benefit of the LASR Labs Winter 2027 programme is the financial and practical support provided to participants.

Successful participants will receive:

  • £15,000 stipend to help cover living expenses in London.
  • Food during the programme.
  • Office space for conducting research.
  • Travel support.
  • Access to an in-person AI safety research environment.
  • Supervision from experienced AI safety researchers.
  • Opportunities to collaborate with other technical researchers.
  • Exposure to leading AI safety organisations and researchers.
  • Opportunities to develop and publish technical research.
  • Opportunities to build professional relationships within the AI safety community.

The programme can therefore provide more than financial support; it can serve as an intensive entry point into the technical AI safety research ecosystem.

Research and Professional Networking Opportunities

Participants will work from the London Initiative for Safe AI, allowing them to interact with AI safety researchers and organisations on a day-to-day basis.

Throughout the programme, LASR Labs organises activities designed to expose participants to the wider AI safety field.

These include:

  • Talks from leading AI safety researchers.
  • A careers fair.
  • Visits to AI research and safety organisations.
  • Opportunities to interact with researchers and practitioners.
  • Participation in events hosted within the London AI safety community.

Previous participants have reportedly used these interactions to find collaborators, mentors and additional career opportunities.

The programme can therefore be particularly useful for applicants who want to establish themselves within the AI safety research ecosystem and develop relationships that may continue beyond the 13-week programme.

AI Safety Research Areas

LASR Labs has previously supported research into several technical areas related to advanced AI safety.

Past projects have included work on:

  • AI control and untrusted monitoring.
  • Data poisoning.
  • Interpretability probes.
  • Chain-of-thought monitoring and faithfulness.
  • Sparse autoencoders.
  • Steganographic collusion.
  • Scheming in frontier AI models.
  • Evaluation awareness in advanced models.

The range of previous topics demonstrates that LASR’s research environment covers multiple approaches to understanding and mitigating risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems.

The programme has also worked with supervisors connected to organisations and academic institutions including Google DeepMind, the UK AI Security Institute, Anthropic and leading UK universities.

Strong Publication Record

LASR Labs may be particularly attractive to applicants who want to build experience in technical research and academic publication.

According to the programme, LASR research papers have been accepted at major machine learning venues and workshops, including NeurIPS, ICLR and ICML workshops.

Recent achievements include:

  • Three LASR papers accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 main conference.
  • One of those papers was selected for an oral presentation.
  • A best paper award at an ICML 2025 workshop.

This publication environment provides participants with the opportunity to develop practical experience in producing research that can potentially reach established academic and technical venues.

Who Should Apply?

LASR Labs is looking for applicants who demonstrate a combination of technical ability, research ability and strong communication skills.

Importantly, the programme does not impose specific formal experience requirements.

Instead, applicants are assessed based on the skills, initiative and evidence they can demonstrate.

1. Technical Ability

Applicants should ideally have strong technical and quantitative capabilities.

Relevant experience may include:

  • Machine learning engineering.
  • Software engineering.
  • Quantitative analysis.
  • Mathematical or statistical work.
  • Building technical systems.
  • Conducting computational experiments.
  • Working with large language models.
  • Developing technical tools.

However, applicants do not necessarily need to have followed a conventional machine learning academic pathway.

2. Research Ability

Applicants should demonstrate an ability to investigate difficult problems and work effectively when the correct approach is not immediately obvious.

LASR particularly values people who can:

  • Experiment systematically.
  • Iterate when initial approaches do not work.
  • Work independently under uncertainty.
  • Identify useful research questions.
  • Develop and test hypotheses.
  • Analyse experimental results.
  • Think critically about evidence.
  • Connect technical research with potential real-world impact.
  • Develop a theory of change for research projects.

Research ability is therefore not simply about having academic research experience. It can also be demonstrated through substantial independent projects, technical experimentation or other forms of problem-solving.

3. Communication Skills

Technical researchers must also be able to explain what their work means.

LASR, therefore, looks for applicants who can clearly communicate:

  • What an experiment was designed to test.
  • What the results demonstrate.
  • What the results do not demonstrate.
  • Why the findings matter.
  • What implications the findings may have.
  • How further research could build on the results.

The programme also highlights the importance of transparent reasoning, particularly when communicating technical research and its implications.

There Are No Specific Experience Requirements

One of the notable features of the LASR Labs opportunity is that applicants are not required to meet a narrowly defined list of academic or professional qualifications.

Instead, successful applicants are expected to have evidence that they can build, investigate, experiment and learn.

Potential evidence may include having:

  • Built a substantial technical system.
  • Produced a research result.
  • Developed a useful tool.
  • Conducted an analysis.
  • Designed and completed an experiment.
  • Developed a proof.
  • Worked on a significant project in machine learning or another field.
  • Worked with large language models.
  • Undertaken serious independent technical projects.
  • Taught themselves machine learning.
  • Transitioned from another discipline into AI-related work.
  • Started an independent research project.

This makes the programme potentially accessible to applicants coming from different academic and professional backgrounds.

Examples of Successful LASR Participants

LASR Labs highlights several examples of people who have previously been strong participants.

One example is an engineer with several years of industry experience who had built and deployed production systems. Although the individual had not initially worked full-time in AI safety research, they had been following the field and wanted to transition into research. They subsequently moved into work at the Australian AI Safety Institute.

Another example is a chemistry PhD student who had spent years independently reading and writing about AI safety. The LASR programme helped the participant turn that independent interest into published technical research. The individual subsequently moved to the Arcadia Alignment Project.

A third example is an undergraduate student who had not yet completed a bachelor’s degree but had established an AI safety group at their university and developed it into a substantial community. Following the LASR programme, the participant progressed towards an internship at Redwood Research.

These examples demonstrate that LASR does not exclusively seek applicants with conventional computer science or AI safety credentials.

Instead, applicants can demonstrate their potential through technical work, research, independent learning, initiative and evidence of commitment to the field.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The programme is intended for people who are interested in pursuing technical AI safety research and who can demonstrate relevant technical, quantitative, research or problem-solving ability.

Academic and Professional Background

Applicants may come from a wide range of backgrounds.

Potentially relevant profiles include:

  • Machine learning engineers.
  • Software engineers.
  • Researchers.
  • PhD students.
  • Master’s students.
  • Undergraduate students.
  • Quantitative researchers.
  • Scientists from other disciplines.
  • Technical professionals transitioning into AI safety.
  • Independent researchers.
  • Self-taught machine learning practitioners.
  • Individuals with substantial experience working with large language models.

A computer science or AI degree is not explicitly required by the programme information.

Likewise, previous AI safety employment is not presented as a mandatory requirement.

The strongest applications are likely to demonstrate evidence of technical capability, initiative and the ability to conduct meaningful research.

Nationality and Geographic Eligibility

The information provided by LASR Labs does not specify a restricted list of eligible nationalities or countries.

The programme is conducted in person in London, United Kingdom, so applicants should be prepared to participate full-time in London for the entire 13-week programme and should consider any applicable UK immigration, visa or work-authorisation requirements relevant to their circumstances.

Applicants from different countries and continents can therefore consider applying, provided they can satisfy the practical and legal requirements for participating in an in-person programme in the United Kingdom.

The programme’s published information also does not state that applicants must belong to a particular race or ethnicity. LASR instead encourages people from underrepresented backgrounds who are interested in the work not to rule themselves out because of doubts about their candidacy.

Why Applicants Should Consider LASR Labs

The Winter 2027 cohort could be particularly valuable for people seeking to move from general technical work into AI safety research.

Some of the major advantages include:

Intensive Research Experience

Participants spend 13 weeks working full-time on an actual AI safety research project rather than simply attending lectures or completing coursework.

Mentorship

Teams receive supervision from experienced AI safety researchers, providing participants with direct feedback throughout the research process.

Publication Potential

Participants work towards producing research that can potentially become a preprint, workshop paper or conference paper.

Strong Technical Environment

Working alongside AI safety researchers and organisations provides participants with exposure to current research practices and technical debates.

Career Development

The programme can help participants understand different career pathways within AI safety while providing opportunities to meet researchers, organisations and potential collaborators.

Financial Support

The £15,000 stipend is designed to support participants’ living expenses in London, while additional programme support includes food, office space and travel.

Research Prioritisation

Participants receive structured exposure to different technical AI safety research directions, helping them develop the ability to assess which research questions may be especially valuable.

What Kind of Candidate Is LASR Looking For?

A strong candidate does not necessarily need to have an impressive collection of academic credentials.

Instead, applicants should focus on demonstrating evidence of what they can actually do.

For example, a candidate could strengthen their application by showing:

  1. A substantial project they have personally built or completed.
  2. Technical competence through software, machine learning, quantitative or computational work.
  3. Research initiative demonstrated through an independent investigation.
  4. Experience with LLMs, whether professionally, academically or independently.
  5. Ability to learn independently, particularly where the applicant has taught themselves new technical concepts.
  6. Clear communication, including the ability to explain technical findings.
  7. Evidence of persistence, particularly when working on difficult problems without obvious solutions.
  8. An interest in AI safety supported by actual engagement rather than simply general enthusiasm.
  9. A focus on impact, including the ability to explain why a research project could matter.

Applicants should not assume that they are unqualified simply because they do not have a traditional AI safety background.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the LASR Labs Winter 2027 cohort is 20 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT.

Applicants should submit their applications before the stated deadline rather than waiting until the final hours, particularly because they may need time to prepare detailed information about their technical projects, research experience and motivation.

How to Apply

Interested applicants can submit their applications through the official LASR Labs application form.

Application deadline: 20 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT

Programme dates: 11 January to 9 April 2027

Programme location: London, United Kingdom

Programme duration: 13 weeks

Stipend: £15,000

Application: Apply for the LASR Labs Winter 2027 Cohort

APPLY HERE

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although there are no rigid formal experience requirements, applicants should use their application to provide concrete evidence of their ability.

Highlight What You Have Built

Instead of simply listing skills, explain what you have actually created or accomplished.

This could be:

  • A machine learning model.
  • A software system.
  • A research project.
  • An analysis.
  • A technical tool.
  • An experiment.
  • A substantial university project.
  • An independent technical project.

Demonstrate Initiative

LASR specifically values people who have taken meaningful steps independently.

If you taught yourself machine learning, started an AI safety project, experimented with LLMs or pursued research outside your formal studies, explain what you did and what you learned.

Explain Your Research Thinking

Do not only describe what you worked on. Explain how you approached the problem.

For example, discuss:

  • The question you were trying to answer.
  • Why the question mattered.
  • Your hypothesis.
  • Your methodology.
  • What you expected to find.
  • What actually happened.
  • How you responded to unexpected results.
  • What you would do differently in a future experiment.

Show Your Ability to Learn

AI safety is a rapidly developing research field. Demonstrating that you can quickly learn unfamiliar concepts and apply them to difficult problems can be valuable.

Avoid Self-Rejection

LASR Labs specifically encourages interested applicants, particularly those from underrepresented groups, not to exclude themselves prematurely because they doubt the strength of their candidacy.

If you can demonstrate technical ability, research potential and genuine interest in the field, it may be worthwhile to apply even if your background does not perfectly match the examples of previous participants.

Conclusion

The LASR Labs Winter 2027 cohort offers an intensive pathway into technical AI safety research for applicants who want to work on concrete questions surrounding the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence.

Running from 11 January to 9 April 2027, the 13-week programme combines research training, hands-on experimentation, mentorship, professional networking and publication opportunities. Participants will work in small teams under experienced supervision and take a research project from proposal through experimentation and analysis to a potential publication.

The programme is also notable for its flexible approach to applicant backgrounds. LASR Labs does not require a specific degree, professional history or number of years of experience. Instead, it looks for evidence of technical ability, quantitative skills, research potential, initiative, experimentation and clear communication.

With a £15,000 stipend, additional food, office space and travel support, as well as access to London’s AI safety research ecosystem, the programme could be a significant opportunity for engineers, researchers, students and independent technical practitioners seeking to build a career in AI safety.

item.content:encoded:
University College London (UCL) is inviting applications for two fully funded four-year PhD studentships focusing on social networks, stereotypes and social inequalities, offering an exceptional research opportunity for quantitatively oriented social scientists interested in understanding how stereotypes can shape educational experiences, peer relationships, well-being and inequality.

The studentships form part of an European Research Council (ERC) Starting Grant project titled “Applied stereotypes, social networks, and self-fulfilling prophecies: How stereotypes reinforce social inequalities.” The project is led by Dr Zsófia Boda and will investigate how stereotypes are applied between individuals, particularly among pupils, and how these interpersonal perceptions may contribute to unequal outcomes.

Successful candidates will be based at the Quantitative Social Science centre within UCL’s Social Research Institute, Institute of Education, in London. The advertised studentships are fully funded for four years and explicitly cover either home or international tuition fees, making the opportunity accessible to applicants from outside the United Kingdom as well as UK candidates.

The official closing date is 1 September 2026, while applications for the planned 1 October 2026 start are being considered on a rolling basis. Candidates interested in the positions should therefore apply as early as possible rather than waiting until the final deadline.

UCL PhD Studentships 2026 at a Glance

University: University College London
Department: School of Education / Social Research Institute
Research Centre: Quantitative Social Science
Location: London, United Kingdom
Reference Number: B16-02225
Number of Studentships: Two
Study Pattern: Full-time
Funding Period: Four years
Funding Status: Fully funded, including home or international tuition fees
Research Area: Social networks, stereotypes, education and social inequalities
Project: Applied stereotypes, social networks, and self-fulfilling prophecies: How stereotypes reinforce social inequalities
Principal Investigator: Dr Zsófia Boda
Expected Start Date: 1 October 2026
Application Deadline: 1 September 2026
Applications: Considered on a rolling basis.

About University College London

University College London is a major research-intensive university based in London and has a substantial international community of students and researchers.

The PhD candidates will become part of UCL’s Social Research Institute, an interdisciplinary centre bringing together researchers from sociology, psychology, social science, economics and related disciplines. Its areas of research include social inequalities, education, employment, migration, gender, families, cultural and social psychology, longitudinal research, advanced quantitative methods and social mobility.

UCL states that its Social Research Institute provides doctoral students with a multidisciplinary and multi-method research environment, comprehensive research training and opportunities to engage with researchers across UCL’s wider academic community.

The Institute of Education also provides an extensive doctoral research environment, including research seminars, doctoral training, methodological courses, workshops and opportunities for students to develop specialist research skills.

About the ERC-Funded Research Project

The two studentships are connected to an ERC Starting Grant examining the relationship between stereotypes, interpersonal perceptions, social networks and persistent social inequalities.

The project’s central focus is the concept of “applied stereotypes.”

Stereotypes are commonly understood as beliefs or assumptions about social groups. These beliefs may relate to ethnicity, gender, social class or other social categories.

However, the project moves beyond examining stereotypes simply as general beliefs about groups.

Instead, it asks an important question:

What happens when one individual actually applies a stereotype to another specific person?

The project therefore seeks to understand how stereotypes operate within real social relationships and whether those perceptions can affect educational achievement, motivation, well-being, aspirations and social connections.

According to the research framing, two particularly important dimensions of stereotypes are warmth and competence. Warmth can relate to perceptions such as whether someone is kind, trustworthy or generous, while competence can involve perceptions of whether someone is capable, knowledgeable, confident or intelligent.

Why Applied Stereotypes Matter

The project begins from the concern that members of minority or disadvantaged groups may sometimes be perceived as less warm, less competent or both compared with members of socially dominant groups.

Such perceptions may influence expectations.

For example, if peers consistently perceive a pupil as less capable because of assumptions associated with that person’s social background, those perceptions may potentially affect:

  • The pupil’s friendships and peer relationships;
  • How other students interact with them;
  • Academic motivation;
  • Aspirations;
  • Confidence;
  • Psychological well-being;
  • Educational performance; and
  • Opportunities to participate fully in school social networks.

Over time, these processes may contribute to self-fulfilling prophecies, whereby expectations influence interactions and those interactions subsequently contribute to outcomes that appear to confirm the original stereotype.

The wider ERC project therefore seeks to understand how stereotypes may help reproduce social inequalities and, crucially, under what circumstances harmful stereotyping can be weakened or avoided.

A Social Network Approach to Stereotyping

One of the most distinctive aspects of the project is its use of social network analysis.

Rather than treating perceptions as characteristics belonging to only one individual, the researchers will conceptualize applied stereotypes as relationships between two people.

For example:

Pupil A may consider Pupil B highly competent, while Pupil C may perceive the same Pupil B very differently.

This means that perceptions are not necessarily uniform.

By examining who perceives whom as warm or competent, researchers can construct networks of interpersonal judgments across entire classrooms.

These networks can then be analysed alongside friendship networks and other peer relationships to investigate how stereotypes are formed, transmitted and potentially reinforced within social environments.

Main Research Aims

The PhD students will contribute to two major empirical objectives within the project.

1. Understanding How Group Stereotypes Are Applied to Individuals

Researchers will investigate whether general stereotypes associated with particular social groups are systematically applied to specific pupils.

The project will examine questions such as:

  • Are students from different social backgrounds perceived differently by their classmates?
  • Who is most likely to apply stereotypes to other students?
  • Under what circumstances are stereotypes more or less likely to influence interpersonal judgments?
  • Do friendship and other peer relationships reduce or reinforce stereotyping?
  • How do perceptions of warmth and competence develop across classroom networks?

2. Investigating Self-Fulfilling Prophecies

The second major objective is to determine whether applied stereotypes ultimately affect pupil outcomes.

Researchers will explore whether other people’s perceptions can influence areas such as:

  • Well-being;
  • Motivation;
  • Educational aspirations;
  • Academic performance;
  • Peer relationships; and
  • Social integration.

The project’s broader goal is to understand whether these interpersonal processes contribute to persistent inequalities between social groups.

Potential Research Questions for PhD Candidates

The studentships provide room for candidates to shape their individual research according to their disciplinary background, interests and methodological expertise.

Questions highlighted in the advertised project include:

  1. Are pupils from different backgrounds systematically perceived differently by their peers?
  2. What role do friendships and other peer relationships play in determining how stereotypes are applied?
  3. How do judgments about warmth and competence spread through social networks?
  4. How do applied stereotypes affect pupil well-being?
  5. Can peer perceptions influence motivation?
  6. Can perceptions of competence affect academic achievement?
  7. Under what circumstances can pupils avoid being subjected to harmful group stereotypes?

Candidates are therefore not expected simply to execute a completely predetermined PhD topic. The project team specifically welcomes students bringing their own research interests and ideas within the overall scope of the ERC project.

Research Methods and Quantitative Training

Advanced quantitative analysis will be central to the studentships.

PhD researchers will use sophisticated statistical and social-network methods to investigate relationships between individuals and changes in those relationships over time.

A particularly important methodology will be longitudinal social network analysis, including stochastic actor-oriented models.

Applicants are not required to already be experts in social network analysis.

The advertisement states that students will receive training in social network analysis, with hands-on support available from the supervisor and senior members of the research team throughout the PhD.

This makes the studentships potentially suitable for candidates who already have strong general quantitative skills but have not previously specialized in network modelling.

Data Collection in English Secondary Schools

The successful PhD candidates will not work exclusively with existing datasets.

They will also contribute to the development and implementation of a major panel data collection in English secondary schools.

This data collection is particularly significant because the project aims to directly measure applied stereotypes among pupils.

The PhD students may contribute to several stages of the research process, including:

  • Measurement development;
  • Questionnaire design;
  • Sample selection;
  • Communication and coordination with schools;
  • Organization and administration of data collection;
  • Data coding;
  • Data cleaning; and
  • Preparation of datasets for statistical analysis.

This provides candidates with extensive practical experience across the research lifecycle rather than limiting doctoral training to secondary data analysis.

Academic Publications and Research Outputs

Successful students will also be expected to contribute to academic publications resulting from the research.

Candidates may prepare academic manuscripts both:

  • As a lead author; and
  • As a contributing co-author with other members of the project team.

This collaborative structure can provide valuable experience in academic publishing and team-based research during the doctorate.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity is intended for highly motivated candidates from the social sciences, broadly defined.

A particularly strong candidate would combine:

  • Genuine interest in social inequalities;
  • Interest in education;
  • Interest in interpersonal and social networks;
  • Strong quantitative research skills;
  • Curiosity about stereotypes and social psychology;
  • Ability to work with complex data;
  • Willingness to collaborate across disciplines; and
  • Enthusiasm for conducting original empirical research.

Applicants from backgrounds such as sociology, psychology and education are explicitly encouraged, although candidates from other related disciplines may also be considered.

Academic Qualification Requirements

Applicants are preferred to have, or be close to obtaining, a first-class Master’s degree or equivalent in an appropriate discipline.

Relevant fields include:

  • Sociology;
  • Psychology;
  • Education; or
  • A closely related social-science discipline.

Candidates must also satisfy UCL’s standard admission requirements for postgraduate research study.

UCL’s Social Science MPhil/PhD normally requires a Master’s degree from a UK university in an appropriate subject, or an equivalent qualification from a recognized institution outside the UK. UCL notes that the majority of successful applicants to the broader programme hold at least a Merit at Master’s level, although this particular studentship advert expresses a preference for a first-class Master’s or equivalent.

Quantitative Skills Requirement

Strong quantitative skills are essential.

Applicants should be comfortable using statistical techniques and should preferably already understand commonly used regression methods.

The advertisement specifically gives examples including:

  • Linear regression; and
  • Logistic regression.

Candidates should therefore be able to demonstrate that they understand quantitative research rather than simply expressing a willingness to learn statistics from the beginning.

Is Previous Social Network Analysis Experience Required?

No.

Existing experience with social network analysis is considered an advantage, but it is not an essential requirement.

This distinction is important for applicants who have strong statistical backgrounds but have not previously worked with network data.

Training in relevant network-analysis techniques will be provided as part of the PhD.

R Programming Requirements

Experience using R for statistical analysis is desirable.

Applicants who do not already have extensive experience with R may still be considered, but they must demonstrate a clear willingness to learn and use R during the doctorate.

Candidates with existing experience in R, statistical programming, quantitative data management or computational social science should therefore highlight this clearly in their application.

Interdisciplinary Research

A willingness to undertake interdisciplinary research is explicitly required.

The project brings together concepts and methods from fields including:

  • Sociology;
  • Social psychology;
  • Education;
  • Quantitative social science;
  • Network science; and
  • Inequality research.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable engaging with theories and literature from disciplines beyond their original academic specialization.

Personal and Professional Skills Required

The successful candidates should demonstrate strong:

  • Organizational skills;
  • Interpersonal skills;
  • Time-management skills;
  • Independent working ability;
  • Team-working ability; and
  • Communication skills.

These qualities will be particularly important because students will participate in a collaborative research project involving schools, research participants, supervisors and other members of the project team.

English Language Requirements

Candidates must possess fluency and clarity in spoken English together with strong written English.

Applicants are also required to meet UCL’s formal English-language requirements for the relevant doctoral programme.

The UCL Social Science MPhil/PhD currently lists English Language Level 4 as the applicable standard. International applicants should consult UCL’s official English-language guidance to determine the accepted tests and scores corresponding to this level.

Funding: What Does “Fully Funded” Mean?

The advertised positions are described as fully funded four-year PhD studentships.

Importantly, the advertisement explicitly states that the funding covers home or international tuition fees.

This means international applicants do not have to be eligible for UK “home” fee status in order to compete for the studentships.

Applicants should rely on the formal studentship offer for the exact financial package applicable to the successful candidate. The advertisement confirms full funding and tuition-fee coverage but does not provide a specific stipend figure in the indexed vacancy text, so applicants should avoid relying on unofficial third-party estimates of annual living support.

International Applicants Are Eligible

A major advantage of the opportunity is that it is open to both home and international candidates.

UCL’s wider Social Research Institute similarly welcomes postgraduate researchers from around the world, and its research-degree information provides country-specific guidance for applicants holding international qualifications.

There is therefore no requirement in the advertised studentship that applicants must be UK citizens.

Duration and Start Date

Each studentship is funded for four years.

Applications are currently being considered for a planned start date of:

1 October 2026

The advertisement states that applications for this start date will be reviewed on a rolling basis.

Applicants who meet the criteria should therefore submit their expression of interest promptly.

Application Deadline

The official UCL vacancy lists the closing date as:

1 September 2026

Because applications are also being considered on a rolling basis for the October start, candidates are strongly advised not to wait until the deadline.

How to Apply

The vacancy instructs candidates to send an expression of interest directly to Dr Zsófia Boda.

The email should be sent to:

info@zsofiaboda.com

The subject line must be:

ERC PhD Studentship

Applicants should attach three separate PDF documents to the email.

Required Application Documents

1. Short CV

Candidates must submit a concise CV with a maximum length of two pages.

Any academic publications can be included.

However, applicants should note that having published academic papers is not a requirement.

The PDF should be named:

LASTNAME_CV.pdf

2. Research Statement

Candidates must submit a research statement of approximately one to two pages.

This statement should explain:

  • Why the applicant is a strong fit for the project;
  • How their academic and methodological background aligns with the studentship;
  • Their substantive research interests;
  • Relevant quantitative research experience; and
  • A potential research idea they would be interested in developing within the overall project.

The file should be titled:

LASTNAME_STATEMENT.pdf

3. Writing Sample

Applicants must also provide a piece of written academic work demonstrating their capacity to conduct original research.

Suitable examples include:

  • A published research article;
  • An unpublished research paper;
  • A chapter from a Master’s thesis;
  • A dissertation chapter; or
  • Another piece of work containing original research.

The PDF should be titled:

LASTNAME_WRITING_SAMPLE.pdf.

What Should You Put in the Research Statement?

The research statement is likely to be one of the most important components of the application.

Applicants should avoid writing a generic motivation statement.

Instead, they should demonstrate a clear connection between their own profile and the project’s substantive and methodological objectives.

A strong statement should explain:

  1. Why you are interested in stereotypes and social inequalities.
  2. Why peer relationships or social networks are relevant to your interests.
  3. Which substantive outcome interests you most, such as educational performance, motivation, well-being or social integration.
  4. Your previous quantitative research training.
  5. Which statistical methods you already know.
  6. Your experience with R or other statistical software.
  7. Any previous exposure to survey design, longitudinal analysis or network analysis.
  8. A focused research question that could be investigated within the broader ERC project.
  9. Why UCL’s Quantitative Social Science environment is particularly suitable for your doctoral development.

The advert explicitly welcomes candidates bringing their own ideas to the project, so the statement should demonstrate intellectual independence while remaining closely aligned with the project’s overall objectives.

Why the Quantitative Social Science Centre Matters

The students will work within UCL’s Quantitative Social Science research environment in the Social Research Institute.

The wider institute has expertise in areas including:

  • Social inequalities;
  • Social mobility;
  • Education;
  • Longitudinal analysis;
  • Gender;
  • Cultural and social psychology;
  • Migration and ethnicity;
  • Labour-market behaviour;
  • Advanced quantitative research methods; and
  • Mixed-method social research.

Doctoral students also have access to research seminars, methodological training and wider doctoral-skills development opportunities across UCL.

The Wider Significance of the Research

The project addresses an important challenge within contemporary social science: understanding why social inequalities can persist even where formal institutions seek to provide equal opportunities.

Stereotypes can operate through everyday interpersonal interactions rather than only through explicit discriminatory decisions.

School peer networks provide an especially valuable environment for studying these processes because adolescence is a period when:

  • Social identities develop;
  • Peer relationships become increasingly important;
  • Academic aspirations are shaped;
  • Friendship networks evolve;
  • Students compare themselves with others; and
  • Perceptions formed by peers may affect confidence and behaviour.

The ERC-funded project aims to develop new evidence on these interpersonal mechanisms and ultimately improve understanding of the conditions under which harmful stereotyping can be reduced.

The broader project has received approximately €1.5 million in ERC Starting Grant support and is designed to investigate stereotyping among pupils in English secondary schools, with research examining how perceptions may contribute to social inequalities.

Equality, Diversity and Inclusion

UCL states that it is committed to equality of opportunity and to creating a fair and inclusive academic community.

The studentship advertisement particularly encourages applications from groups that may be underrepresented within UCL, including candidates from Black, Asian and ethnic minority backgrounds, disabled candidates and LGBTQI+ candidates.

This is an encouragement to apply rather than an eligibility restriction: applicants are not required to belong to any particular racial, ethnic or demographic group.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

Candidates should treat the expression of interest as a competitive doctoral-research application rather than a standard employment application.

To strengthen an application:

  • Keep the CV focused on research, methods, education and relevant professional experience.
  • Highlight Master’s dissertation work involving quantitative analysis.
  • Specify statistical techniques you can already use.
  • Mention experience with R, Stata, Python, SPSS or other analytical software where relevant.
  • Clearly identify experience with linear or logistic regression.
  • Highlight any work involving longitudinal, relational or network data.
  • Demonstrate a genuine substantive interest in inequality, education and social relationships.
  • Propose a realistic and analytically interesting research idea.
  • Show evidence of independent research capability in the writing sample.
  • Demonstrate that you can contribute effectively to collaborative data collection in schools.
  • Submit well before the final deadline because applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Important Dates

Applications currently open: Yes
Application review: Rolling basis
Final closing date: 1 September 2026
Expected PhD start: 1 October 2026

Conclusion

The UCL PhD studentships on social networks, stereotypes and social inequalities provide an outstanding opportunity for quantitatively skilled social-science graduates who want to investigate some of the mechanisms through which inequality can be reproduced in educational environments.

Two candidates will join an ambitious ERC-funded research project examining how pupils perceive one another, how stereotypes are applied within social networks and whether those perceptions can produce self-fulfilling consequences for academic performance, motivation, well-being and social relationships.

The studentships are particularly attractive because they combine theoretical social-science research with advanced quantitative methodology, original longitudinal data collection, social network analysis and opportunities to publish collaboratively.

Both UK and international candidates are eligible, and the four-year studentships are described as fully funded, including home or international tuition fees. Applicants should ideally hold or be completing a first-class Master’s degree in sociology, psychology, education or a related discipline and must demonstrate strong quantitative skills, interdisciplinary interest and the ability to meet UCL’s doctoral admission requirements.

Candidates must submit a two-page CV, a one-to-two-page research statement and a research writing sample as separate PDFs by email, using the subject line “ERC PhD Studentship.”

The final deadline is 1 September 2026, but applications for the 1 October 2026 start are being considered on a rolling basis, making early submission advisable.
